name: Isoxsuprine

lead: Isoxsuprine is a prescription vasodilator and beta2 agonist. It has been used for circulation problems, for slowing premature labour, and in horses for hoof conditions.
In appearance circles it comes up as a beta agonist that people connect with fat loss, though its documented uses are circulatory and obstetric.

paras: It stimulates beta2-adrenergic receptors, relaxing the smooth muscle of blood vessels and the uterus. Beta stimulation in general raises circulating free fatty acids, which is the basis of the fat-loss interest.
Reported effects include dizziness, flushing, fast heart rate, low blood pressure and nausea. It is a prescription drug, and Grokipedia reports US approval of its products was withdrawn in 2020.

angle.text: Isoxsuprine is a vasodilator and beta agonist, and people interested in leaner physiques discuss it because of that beta-agonist class. Its documented uses are circulatory and obstetric.

lead: Isoxsuprine is a beta-adrenergic agonist and peripheral vasodilator that relaxes vascular and uterine smooth muscle [1]. It has been used in people for circulation problems and to slow premature labour, and in horses for hoof conditions such as navicular disease [1][2].

Its place in appearance discussions comes from its beta-agonist class: beta-adrenergic stimulation raises circulating free fatty acids, and some people interested in fat loss ask whether related drugs could help. Research on isoxsuprine itself has focused on circulation and uterine uses rather than body composition.

Published studies include a Cochrane review of beta2-agonists for period pain, randomised trials in oral submucous fibrosis and vasculogenic impotence, and a trial in navicular disease in horses [3][4][5][6].
infobox: Prescription drug; US approval withdrawn 2020 per Grokipedia [2]

paras: In people, isoxsuprine has been used as a vasodilator in conditions such as Raynaud's phenomenon and cerebral vascular insufficiency, and as a tocolytic for preterm labour [1][7][8]. A 1974 clinical trial examined it as an oral vasodilator [9].

In horses it is used for hoof problems including navicular disease and laminitis, based on the idea that it improves hoof circulation; a double-blind study evaluated it for navicular disease [1][6]. It is a prohibited substance in FEI competition [1].
Reported effects include dizziness, flushing, faster heart rate, low blood pressure, nausea and nervousness; caution is advised with other blood-pressure-affecting drugs [1][2].

Isoxsuprine is a phenylethanolamine derivative that acts as a beta2-adrenergic agonist, relaxing smooth muscle directly [1]. Earlier physiology work examined how adrenergic-stimulating agents change plasma growth hormone, insulin and free fatty acid levels in people [10].

Grokipedia reports US FDA approval in 1959 under the brand Vasodilan and a Drug Efficacy Study Implementation review that led to withdrawal of approval of oral products in 2020 [2]. Early obstetric reports date to the 1960s [11].

A Cochrane review found trials of beta2-agonists, including oral isoxsuprine, for primary dysmenorrhoea [3]. A randomised trial in 40 people with oral submucous fibrosis compared isoxsuprine with dexamethasone and hyaluronidase injections [4]. A randomised crossover study compared yohimbine plus isoxsuprine with pentoxifylline in vasculogenic impotence [5]. A 2022 study compared oral nifedipine with parenteral isoxsuprine for arresting preterm labour [12]. A small phase 1/2 trial tested isoxsuprine in multiple sclerosis relapses [13]. No studies on isoxsuprine for body-fat reduction were found.
